q.young: Does it wake you up at night?
q.older: Does the discomfort wake you up at night?

candidates.why: Item 1: source 6's 'pain waking from sleep' and source 7's 'Nocturnal pain' as the concrete event the packet says a child remembers, presence only, no grading.

q.young: Does it hurt when you are in bed?
q.older: Does your back hurt when you are lying in bed?

candidates.why: Item 1: the second half of the item title, carrying source 2's 'Night pain' and source 4's night pain without the banned grading word 'unrelenting'.

q.young: Does it hurt when you are sitting quietly?
q.older: Does it hurt even when you are resting and not moving?

candidates.why: Item 2: source 2's 'pain at rest' and source 4's 'pain at rest', reworded around the banned word by naming the state (sitting quietly / resting) instead.

q.young: Does it hurt when you are not moving?
q.older: Does the discomfort stay even when you are not moving around?

candidates.why: Item 2: source 3's 'change with activity or rest' as its own atom, deliberately unfused from item 1 per decision 4, and phrased as the inverse of item 10.

q.young: Do you feel hot or shivery?
q.older: Have you been feeling hot or shivery?

candidates.why: Item 3: the child's half of source 1's 'Fever' and source 4's 'Fever, chills' behind source 2's discitis warning; reuses the shared fact per decision 8, never a measured temperature.

q.young: Has going to the bathroom been different today?
q.older: Has going to the bathroom felt different since your back started hurting?

candidates.why: Item 4: source 6's 'Change to urinary or bowel habit' asked as change rather than accident, in the app's existing 'bathroom' register, floored at 8 as judgement.

q.young: Does it feel different when you need to pee?
q.older: Does it feel different when you go to the bathroom?

candidates.why: Item 4: source 4's 'difficulties urinating' reached through the tummy packet's 'pee' without naming incontinence, enuresis or fault; asks for difference, never what happened.

q.young: Do your legs feel wobbly?
q.older: Do your legs feel weak or wobbly when you stand up?

candidates.why: Item 5: source 2's 'weakness' and source 4's 'leg weakness' in the packet's ruled vocabulary (wobbly/weak, never give way or buckle), symptom not examined deficit.

q.young: Do your legs feel weak?
q.older: Have your legs felt weak or wobbly lately?

candidates.why: Item 5: the child's half of source 1's 'motor disturbances of the extremities', with source 2's and source 4's grading adjectives stripped so it stays askable.

q.young: Does your leg feel like it went to sleep?
q.older: Do your legs ever feel fuzzy or tingly, like pins and needles?

candidates.why: Item 6: source 1's 'sensory disturbances' reached through the packet's ruled child words; young leans on 'gone to sleep', older uses tingly and pins because SENSATIONS.tingly proves 8-12s hold it.

q.young: Does anywhere feel fuzzy or funny?
q.older: Does your leg ever feel fuzzy or gone to sleep?

candidates.why: Item 6: same criterion asked as whether it happens rather than which adjective fits, avoiding the menu the packet warns turns the item into a vocabulary test.

q.young: Does the discomfort go down your leg?
q.older: Does the discomfort go down your back and into your leg?

candidates.why: Item 7: source 1's 'Radicular pain' as one pain that moves, which the body map cannot record; uses 'goes down your leg', never radiates, shoots or the condition name.

q.young: Do you feel it in your leg too?
q.older: Does the discomfort from your back go all the way down your leg?

candidates.why: Item 7: source 3's radiculopathy line, with source 4's 'bilateral' qualifier dropped so the question does not invite a child to report the shape of the question.

q.young: Is it hard to get moving in the morning?
q.older: When you wake up, is it hard to get moving?

candidates.why: Item 8: source 2's 'Morning stiffness' and source 7's 'worse in morning' as a time pattern, presence only because source 4's 30-60 minutes cannot be timed by a child.

q.young: Does your back feel tight when you wake up?
q.older: Does your back feel hard to move when you first wake up?

candidates.why: Item 8: source 3's 'inflammatory symptoms (morning stiffness)' phrased as hard to get moving rather than the older-tier-only SENSATIONS word 'stiff'.

q.young: Did you fall or lift something heavy?
q.older: Did you have a fall, or lift something heavy?

candidates.why: Item 9: re-sources the shipped back-fell, fall half from five sources and lifting half from source 1's Table 2, with source 2's 'significant' grading not carried.

q.young: Did you hurt your back doing something?
q.older: Did something happen to your back, like a fall or carrying something heavy?

candidates.why: Item 9: source 3's 'trauma (acute macrotrauma, repetitive microtrauma... recent/remote)' as a plain event question, not duration-restricted because a remote fall still counts.

q.young: Is it worse when you move around?
q.older: Does your back hurt more when you are moving around?

candidates.why: Item 10: re-sources back-worse-move from source 3's 'mechanical symptoms (worse during or after activity)'; new fact, never worse-on-exertion, which is the chest discriminator.

q.young: Does moving make it hurt more?
q.older: Does the discomfort get worse when you move around?

candidates.why: Item 10: source 1's 'Onset of back pain associated with exercise' kept neutral because the same raw fact is reassuring in source 3 and alarming in source 1; no instruction to move.

q.young: Is it worse when you sit down?
q.older: Does your back hurt more when you have been sitting down?

candidates.why: Item 11: re-sources back-worse-sit from source 1 Table 2's 'sitting' and source 3's aggravating factors; the packet records this as its weakest citation and ranks it last.

q.young: Does it stop you from playing?
q.older: Is it stopping you from doing things you normally do?

candidates.why: Item 12: source 2's 'Interference with function e.g. school, play, sport' anchored on play and normal activity, because the packet bans school as the anchor in a hospital.

q.young: Is it hard to do the things you like?
q.older: Has it stopped you doing things you usually do at home?

candidates.why: Item 12: source 3's 'current level of function of the child' and source 6's 'Functional limitations', with a home anchor offered against the packet's open worry that 'normally do' is vague at four.

q.young: Do you play sports or dance?
q.older: Do you do sports, dancing, or gymnastics most days?

candidates.why: Item 13: source 2's 'Competitively sporty / dancer' and source 1's evidence-graded 'Competitive sports', asked as what the child does and never as the cause of the pain.

q.young: Is it hard to walk?
q.older: Is it hard to walk around right now?

candidates.why: Item 14: source 2's 'Gait disturbance' and source 6's 'inability to walk or weight bear', reusing limb-use per decision 8 and using the packet's prescribed phrasing over 'can you walk'.
